The Cost of Reliable Near-Optimal Set Maintenance with Arriving Arms Deqi Zheng ∗ Xiaoyang Xu ∗ Qiuzhen College, Tsinghua University Yuhong Yang † Yau Mathematical Sciences Center, Tsinghua University October 15, 2026 Abstract We study reliable maintenance of all relatively near-optimal arms while collecting rewards when new arms arrive exogenously and remain available. Reward laws are stationary, but arrivals change the membership boundary. Reporting progress is measured by cumulative unresolved arm time outside a prescribed boundary band, with simultaneous correctness of all labels. One uncertain arrival can obstruct many earlier certifications. A common-reference lower bound quantifies this effect, and matching worst-schedule area bounds yield an arrival-growth boundary for joint sublinear performance. On specified repeated-update families, temporary membership tasks impose rapid-maintenance regret costs, while separate constructions attain deferred and intermediate service levels. We develop Flexible Certificate-Cost Planning (F-CCP) as a tunable implementation. It combines sequential evidence and local certificate planning with a chosen reward kernel and separate observable budgets for reward and certification. Its guarantees include label reliability, unconditional expected-regret protection, and service-rate area bounds that retain budget rejections. Fixed-checkpoint and activation-budgeted constructions remain distinct analytical witnesses. Frozen paired experiments show lower mean costs in many finite-budget comparisons, together with exceptions, heavier regret tails, and nonzero reporting failures. These results do not characterize a general regret–maintenance frontier. Keywords: sequential experimentation; arriving arms; near-optimal set maintenance; dynamic regret; confidence sequences. 1 Introduction Sequential experiments often acquire new candidates while earlier ones remain available. An allocation rule must learn which candidates yield high rewards. An experimenter may also need to know which of all available candidates are within a specified tolerance of the current best. These ∗ † The first two authors contributed equally. Corresponding author: yyangsc@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn. 1 objectives need not favor the same observations. A candidate can be sufficiently inferior to receive little reward-driven exploration and still be difficult to classify relative to the near-optimality boundary. We study these objectives together under permanent exogenous arrivals and stationary reward laws. If r ∗ (t) is the largest mean among the arms available at time t, an arm is relatively near-optimal when its mean is at least r ∗ (t) − ε. Reports certify membership, certify exclusion, or leave the arm unresolved. We require one simultaneous correctness event for all labels at all times. To rule out indefinite abstention, we charge the cumulative unresolved time of arms whose means lie more than η from the membership boundary. The question is how much regret is necessary, and how much is attainable, under this reporting requirement. New arrivals affect the task in two ways. An uncertain new candidate may be better than the incumbent by enough to invalidate many existing positive reports. Evidence about that one candidate is then relevant to many reports at once. A later improvement can also make an earlier difficult membership question unnecessary: a candidate close to the old boundary may be far below the new one. Its existing upper confidence bound can be combined with a new reference’s lower bound to certify exclusion. Neither effect requires the reward law of an old arm to change. Our observation model and regret comparator have established precedents. Permanent arrivals form a monotone special case of sleeping-bandit availability (Kleinberg et al., 2010); ballooning bandits already compare reward with the best arm currently available (Ghalme et al., 2021). Exogenous arrivals differ from drawing arms on demand from a reservoir (Berry et al., 1997) and from the disappearing actions of mortal bandits (Chakrabarti et al., 2008). Benchmark improvements here arise from new arms, whereas nonstationary bandits allow the reward distributions of existing arms to change (Besbes et al., 2014; Auer et al., 2019). Sequential allocation and adaptive experimentation have a long statistical history (Robbins, 1952; Lai and Robbins, 1985; Lai, 1987); the expanding set of actions retains that allocation problem and adds an evolving inferential target. For a fixed arm set, identifying every relatively near-optimal arm is the ALL-ε problem (Mason et al., 2020). Joint reward and identification objectives also have established precedents (Degenne et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2026; Cho et al., 2025). Our task requires continuing reports under arrivals, with all-time label reliability and an explicit cumulative cost for unresolved arm time. The distinction concerns the reporting protocol and its cost, rather than a new arriving-arm model. The simultaneous recovery scales used in our lower bounds build on existing information inequalities and multiple-recovery arguments (Kaufmann et al., 2016; Malloy and Nowak, 2014; Jamieson and Jain, 2018). We give three results about maintenance cost. First, a common-reference lower bound shows how one uncertain arrival can obstruct many other certifications. Its information queue accumulates cost over time within one reward environment. Second, we obtain matching worst-schedule orders for cumulative unresolved area, including finite-horizon truncation, and derive the polynomial arrival boundary for jointly sublinear area and expected regret. This worst-case lower bound already occurs in an initial static batch; the common-reference result describes a separate consequence of continuing arrivals. Third, on a specified repeated-update family, rapid resolution of temporary 2 membership tasks has matching inverse-square regret costs. Allowing a constant-factor larger area budget admits a logarithmic regret upper bound. A nonvanishing-probability lower bound holds in one fixed environment under the same cumulative-area requirement. The deferred endpoint has only an upper bound. A separate activation-budgeted witness covers an intermediate interval on a more strongly separated family; the general causal frontier under overlapping arrivals remains open. Fixed checkpoints make attainable costs explicit, but their quotas can consume a moderate budget before useful reports appear. F-CCP uses every observation to update valid reporting evidence and plans one certificate observation at a time. A predictable priority controls the proposed service rate. Separate budgets limit the virtual-index cost of reward choices and of certification, so exploration by the reward kernel does not exhaust the certification account. The resulting guarantees concern reliability, regret protection, and conditional service bounds; the local planning proxy is not a solution of the full statistical allocation problem. The fixed-checkpoint witnesses are retained for their original guarantees in the supplement. The components have precedents. Betting processes provide time-uniform inference for bounded means (Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2024); our particular mixture and its bounded-reward validity are proved explicitly. Thompson sampling supplies a flexible reward rule (Thompson, 1933). MOTS obtains fixed-arm minimax guarantees by modifying sampled scores (Jin et al., 2021). Our protection instead constrains the virtual-index cost of the actual selected action under arrivals, and does not transfer MOTS’s theorem to a cold-temperature Beta rule. Conservative bandits control performance against a fixed baseline (Wu et al., 2016); the two accounts here control index deficits and are not realized shortfalls from a separately run baseline. The spectral accounting and MC-MOSS concentration tools are inputs from the companion work (Temporal Geometry), not a new characterization claimed here. Information about future task expiration also matters. A schedule-specific comparator can defer a temporary question in a way that one causal policy facing an unknown schedule cannot reproduce uniformly. We retain that information distinction and an activation-budgeted intermediate-regime result alongside the general maintenance bounds. The latter uses its own window conditions and is not an optimality claim for F-CCP. Section 2 fixes the joint task and separates task parameters from allocation preferences. Section 3 presents F-CCP and its guarantees. Sections 4 and 5 give the general costs, temporary-task bounds, and information limits. Section 6 evaluates frozen configurations, including mean improvements, tail costs, failed reports, and the corrected same-controller comparison. 2 Model, reliable reports, and maintenance cost 2.1 Observation model and regret Let A be a possibly infinite set of arms. Arm i arrives at time τ i , after which it remains available. At every physical time t = 1, 2, . . ., A t = {i : τ i ≤ t}, 1 ≤ K t = |A t | < ∞. 3 Arbitrary finite batches are allowed, including K T > T at an evaluation endpoint. Each arm has an unknown stationary reward law on [0, 1] with mean r i . Its successive potential observations (Y i,n ) n≥1 are independent and identically distributed, and the streams of different arms are independent. Arrivals are exogenous and independent of both these streams and policy randomization. Unless stated otherwise, each result is for a fixed deterministic arrival schedule. At time t, the policy first receives all current arrivals, then selects one arm I t ∈ A t , observes one reward X t,I t , and finally issues its report. It uses the observed history H t−1 = (A s , I s , X s,I s ) t−1 s=1 and independent randomization. Means, future arrivals, and true membership labels are unavailable P to the policy. With N i (t) = s≤t 1{I s = i}, the physical observation is X t,I t = Y I t ,N It (t−1)+1 . Write r̂ i (n) = n 1 X Y i,s , n s=1 r ∗ (t) = max r i , ∆ i (t) = r ∗ (t) − r i i∈A t (i ∈ A t ). At a deterministic endpoint T , cumulative dynamic regret is R T (π) = T X ∆ I t (t). t=1 This is a sum of mean gaps, random through the policy’s arm selections; ER T is its expectation. The quantity does not compare realized reward sequences. Physical time always counts actual observations. 2.2 Reliable reports and cumulative unresolved time For 0 < ε < 1, the target set is G t ε = {i ∈ A t : ∆ i (t) ≤ ε}. After the current observation, a report partitions all of A t into P t , N t , V t : certified members, certified nonmembers, and unresolved arms. Define E lab = {for all t : P t ⊆ G t ε ⊆ A t \ N t }. A policy is δ-reliable if P(E lab ) ≥ 1 − δ in every allowed reward environment. A positive report may be withdrawn after a new arrival. On the correctness event, a negative report remains valid because r ∗ (t) is nondecreasing and the arm’s mean is stationary. Reliability permits all arms to remain unresolved. For a boundary width 0 < η < 1, define d εi (t) = |∆ i (t) − ε|, U t (η) = X 1{i ∈ V t , d εi (t) > η}, U T (η) = T X t=1 i∈A t 4 U t (η). Every such arm–time pair is charged; the loss is not limited to the time before a first decision. Within the boundary band, unresolved time is exempt, but any label issued there must still be correct. The true distance d εi (t) is used only by the evaluator and in the analysis. In particular, U T = o(T ) requires the time-average number of unresolved separated arms to vanish, rather than only a small unresolved fraction of all arms. The value is +∞ if the feasible class is empty. Full-model label reliability and a family-specific area guarantee are distinct requirements. The lower bounds remain valid when reliability is required only on the lower-bound subfamily. 2.3 How arrivals change the reporting problem For a fixed old arm, ∆ i (t) is nondecreasing, so its true membership can change only from member to nonmember. Its boundary distance |∆ i (t) − ε| need not be monotone. A new candidate can first create uncertainty about the current best mean, obstructing positive certification of many old arms even when those arms remain truly near-optimal. A sufficiently good new reference can later move the boundary past earlier candidates, making their fine classification unnecessary. Sections 4 and 5 quantify these two effects under the same reporting protocol. Arms with close means need not be close to the relative boundary r ∗ (t) − ε. Conversely, a candidate near that boundary can require fine evidence even when its reward gap is appreciable. 5 The algorithm’s observable work set is therefore defined from confidence intervals, not from the evaluator’s true gaps or unresolved area. 3 Flexible certificate-cost planning The reporting task need not receive a fixed fraction of every sampling budget. Evidence obtained while collecting rewards can already certify some arms, and a small amount of additional work can complete other reports. Flexible Certificate-Cost Planning (F-CCP) uses one set of lifetime statistics for both purposes. Its service preference controls how often certification is attempted; two separate budgets protect the reward allocation and reserve capacity for certification. The resulting guarantees concern reliable labels, regret order, and service completion. They do not identify the optimal allocation for every joint regret–area constraint. 3.1 Evidence and current reporting work Order arms by arrival, with a fixed order within each batch. Under the bounded stationary model, every legal predictable choice of preferences, prices, and service actions in F-CCP satisfies P(E lab ) ≥ 1 − δ. On a common event E of this probability, all confidence intervals cover their means at all observed counts, all reports are correct, and every arm in Z t lies in the boundary band. The evidence argument does not require the proxy plan to predict its actual sampling cost. The mixture and checkpoint errors each receive δ/2, and a union bound gives E. Proposition 3.2 (Compatibility endpoint). Fix a legal reward kernel B. If service is off from the start (λ t ≡ 0), β R = ∞, and the complete kernel state, initialization, and random-number source agree with those of B, the two procedures have identical actions, lifetime counts, and regret on every potential reward realization and arrival schedule. This is a same-backend pathwise statement. A common seed in different random-number backends does not provide the required coupling. The colder, guarded F-R preset is distinct from this endpoint. Switching off service after using it does not recreate a baseline’s independent past. Here busy means that the current W t is nonempty after arrivals and before observation. If every current arm has reached its checkpoint, the gap intervals are narrow enough that W t is empty. Each successful service therefore advances a finite remaining checkpoint, and phase accounting bounds the number of busy rounds. This proves the theorem without requiring a cost-optimal plan. An arbitrary predictable λ t preserves label reliability, but completion speed needs the displayed positive lower bound. Corollary 3.5 (Finite-arm completion). Suppose β C > 0 is fixed, busy rounds have a uniform positive service rate, and arrivals eventually stop with finitely many arms. On E, every arm outside the boundary band eventually receives a definite label. This conclusion holds regardless of continuing reward-kernel exploration and its separate ledger consumption. A conservative finite-prefix bound, the compatibility proof, and a one-round obstruction to exact all-environment dominance appear in Supplement S4. Completion on a fixed-confidence event concerns the boundary band; it is not unconditional almost-sure consistency for the exact oracle set. 4 Fundamental costs of continual maintenance 4.1 One uncertain arrival can obstruct many reports The first lower bound retains one reward environment throughout the time axis. It therefore measures a cumulative burden without adding the worst cases of incompatible experiments. Fix 0 < ε ≤ 1/16, 0 < δ ≤ 1/16, and 0 < η < ε/2. An initial reference has Bernoulli mean 1/4 + ε/2. Candidates arrive on any prescribed schedule. In environment zero each has mean p = 1/4; environment j changes only candidate j to mean p + 2ε. All candidates are good in environment zero, with boundary distance ε/2. After candidate j arrives in environment j, every other candidate is bad. It is distinct from F-CCP’s phased service rule and from the fixed-checkpoint witness’s FIFO queue. It imposes no pathwise sampling quota on every candidate. In the stated range q − ≥ 2. Theorem 4.1 (Broadcast uncertainty). For every policy reliable on environment zero and all its one-candidate alternatives, E 0 U T (η) ≥ (3/4 − δ)B T . If B T > 0, then P 0 {U T (η) ≥ B T /4} ≥ 1/4. These conclusions still hold when the policy knows the full arrival schedule, the horizon, and the reference distribution. At a busy time, some deterministic candidate label has expected sample count below q − . Changing that candidate alone has too little history KL to permit positive certification of another candidate with probability at least 1/4. Reliability also bounds incorrect negative reports. The remaining probability must be unresolved. The supplementary argument selects a single infinite schedule; the difficult reward environment is allowed to vary with the endpoint, as required by the stated uniform guarantee. 5 Temporary tasks and limits of the regret–maintenance trade-off 5.1 A repeated-update family We keep the reward environment, arrival schedule, endpoint, and reporting parameters fixed when comparing two area budgets. Choose integers J ≥ 1, M ≥ max{2, J} and 0 < ε ≤ 1/8, 0 < δ ≤ 1/16, Jv ≤ ε/4, 0 < v, 0 < d ≤ v/32, η = d/2. (27) At a e = 1 + eH, e = 0, . . . , J, a reference with mean b e = 1/2 + ev arrives. For each e < J, the same batch contains M candidates with means r e,k = b e − ε + σ e,k d, σ e,k ∈ {−1, +1}. (28) All rewards are Bernoulli and all arms remain available. The last batch contains only its reference, and T = (J + 1)H. The family Θ includes every sign configuration and every within-batch permutation. The policy is not told which arm is the reference. Lower bounds may disclose those identities and the schedule. In its birth window a candidate is good exactly when its sign is positive. Its reward gap is ε − σ e,k d, while its distance to the membership boundary is d. At the next update its gap becomes ε + v − σ e,k d, so both signs are bad, with boundary distance at least v − d. Every reference remains good: the final good set consists of all references. The tasks that distinguish the candidate signs expire even though their arms remain available. The restriction Jv ≤ ε/4 limits the number of updates at any fixed positive improvement size. 5.2 Low area forces enough temporary tasks to finish The lower-bound ingredient permits arbitrary interleaving and stopping. For m independent uniform signs with observation laws P i + , P i − , put κ = max max{D(P i + ∥P i − ), D(P i − ∥P i + )} ∈ (0, ∞). i If a bounded stopping time has at least half the signs determined with prior probability at least 1/2, and all configurations have familywise report error at most δ ≤ 1/16, then E m X i=1 N i ≥ m m log . 1024κ δ 15 (29) Other observations must not encode these signs. The proof factors the conditional posterior after the adaptive sampling and bounded stopping kernels cancel, and combines simultaneous recovery with coordinatewise change of measure (Kaufmann et al., 2016). It does not assume independence of the random sample counts. The product prior is a proof device; the final lower bound concerns a fixed environment. A window that never reaches half-completion contributes at least M H/2 area. Thus, on the event U T (η) ≤ V /8, where V = JM H, at least 3J/4 windows half-complete. A common product prior over all windows turns this area requirement into enough instances of (29). Each candidate observation costs at least ε − d regret, and observations from distinct batches are charged once. This argument does not impose a deadline on every individual batch; the policy can choose where to defer. The heterogeneous completion probabilities and their information-allocation relaxation are given in Supplementary Section S8. In the repeated-update family, suppose a reliable policy satisfies P σ {E lab , U T (η) ≤ V /8} ≥ 1 − δ for every sign configuration. Both still lack the true reward means. Supplementary Theorem S12.1 constructs early and late improvements with the same horizon, area budget, final arm count, and common initial history. Timely service on the late schedule forces an inverse-square cost on the early schedule, while an early-schedule comparator has a logarithmic upper bound. This rules out a universal constant-factor comparison with every separately optimized schedule frontier. It does not rule out an optimal policy for a common causal minimax problem. The interval result belongs to ABM, not to the preference parameter of F-CCP, and leaves smaller budgets and general overlapping arrivals unresolved. 6 Numerical studies 6.1 Protocol and comparisons We study reward performance and the cost of reliable reporting separately. The frozen main suite contains 12 scenarios, 24 configurations and 96 paired replications per scenario and configuration, giving 27,648 records. A subsequent correction of one ALL comparator contributes 1,152 additional records. The original and corrected comparator records are both retained. The primary analysis replaces the original adaptive ALL configuration by its corrected version, leaving 24 configurations and 27,648 records. The scenarios have 2–20 arms and horizons of 12,000–16,000. Eleven use Bernoulli rewards; one 18 uses bounded two-point rewards. The reporting parameters ε and η vary by scenario, while δ = .05 throughout. Supplementary Section S15 gives every arrival time, mean and configuration. Within a replication, all methods share the same potential reward stream for each arm, and the mean labels of arms arriving together are jointly permuted. The action routines receive only revealed arms, past observations and their own randomization; they do not receive the means, future arrivals or evaluation horizon. All failed-report paths remain in every reported mean, area and quantile. The five reward comparators are UCB1, Growing-MOSS, MC-MOSS, Thompson sampling and KL-UCB (Garivier and Cappé, 2011). They make no designated certification pulls and carry the same valid reporter as F-CCP. Thompson sampling uses Beta(1, 1) updates for Bernoulli rewards; its fractional updates for the bounded two-point scenario are an action heuristic, not a correctly specified Bernoulli posterior. F-R uses temperature .5 and reward protection β R = 16 with service disabled. The compatibility configuration F-R-TS-exact instead uses temperature one and no reward guard; it reproduces the specified Thompson rule rather than serving as a second independent comparator. For joint performance we compare the prespecified F configurations with CCP-original, ALL-area and ALL-auto-costmatched. CCP-original is the earlier CCP configuration in this test suite, not the checkpoint method in Supplementary Section S17. The ALL methods are natural retained-history adaptations, rather than implementations of the original FAREAST or (ST ) 2 procedures. The corrected adaptive ALL method uses the same projected-mean sampling price as F-CCP, the same reward kernel and the same two budgets. Its initial implementation returned zero as that price; the correction changes that comparator input alone, with the scenarios, seeds and all F-CCP parameters fixed. The superseded output remains a diagnostic in Supplementary Section S16. Development and testing use separate environments and seeds. The reward configuration was selected by the prespecified equal-weight development mean regret, and the moderate-service configuration was fixed before the main test. No preference, temperature or confidence parameter is selected from the test results. The parameter values in these experiments are not generally in the narrower regime of the minimax lower bound; these comparisons do not validate its asymptotic rate. 6.2 Reward performance with service disabled F-R has a lower mean regret than all five reward comparators in 11 of the 12 scenarios, and a strictly lower mean in 59 of the 60 scenario–comparator comparisons. Its mean is 19.5% below Thompson sampling when the 12 scenario means are averaged with equal weights. This ratio compares two descriptive suite averages; it is not an average of scenario-specific percentage reductions or a risk under one common environment distribution. The gain in this experiment concerns the reward-score configuration and its protection, since the certificate scheduler is disabled. The two-close-arms scenario is an exception. F-R minus Thompson has mean 0.70 and a paired, two-sided 95% approximate t interval [−5.28, 6.68]. Across the full family of 60 prespecified comparisons, 52 one-sided Bonferroni-adjusted upper endpoints are below zero. Under the separate, more permissive margin of 5% of the comparator mean plus two regret units, 54 are below the corresponding threshold. The latter criterion is not zero-margin noninferiority. Its empirical 95th percentile exceeds Thompson’s in the burst, ceiling and larger-pool scenarios in Table 4. Each percentile uses only 96 replications; it should not be read as a precise population tail estimate. F-auto-0.6 produces an incorrect determined label on one of its 1,152 runs; F-R and F-area produce none. Coverage failures and empty intersections also occur: the respective counts are (6, 1) for F-R, (7, 1) for F-auto-0.6, and (8, 0) for F-area. An empty intersection triggers persistent all-unresolved reporting, not successful completion. All these runs enter the cost calculations. Full failure counts, empirical maxima and implementation qualifications appear in Supplementary Sections S15–S16. 7 Discussion Reliable maintenance has costs that reward allocation alone does not measure. An uncertain arrival can obstruct many positive reports, while a later improvement can end a fine membership task. The general lower bounds quantify these effects. The worst-area lower bound answers a different question and is already attained by an initial static batch; the fixed-schedule and terminal-count growth consequences retain different quantifiers. F-CCP adds an implementable choice of emphasis to this task. Its evidence layer uses every observation, its certificate planner proposes a single next observation, and separate accounts control reward and certification costs. Finite guards protect the spectral regret order but can reject service; the area bound retains that rejection cost. Classification priority with no certification guard 22 Table 4: Empirical 95th percentiles of cumulative dynamic regret from 96 replications per method and scenario. These are finite-sample tail summaries, not high-probability regret bounds. Scenario Burst Ceiling Larger pool F-R Thompson 208.887 90.940 237.301 123.069 48.971 184.175 achieves the worst-area order, without being fastest on every instance. A compatibility endpoint recovers a specified baseline from the start under identical state and randomization. The default cold-temperature reward mode has a different contract. The frozen experiments support lower mean reward costs for F-R in most of the specified comparisons and useful finite-budget trade-offs for the service modes. They also show an exception in the two-arm close-mean case, heavier empirical regret tails than Thompson sampling in three environments, and a nonzero label-error record for the balanced mode. Pure-reward improvements cannot be attributed to certificate scheduling that was switched off. The corrected matched-cost ALL comparison is distinct from the retained superseded controller result. These findings concern the frozen suite, not uniform dominance or a general frontier. The activation-budgeted witness characterizes an intermediate interval on a sufficiently separated family, with an additive reward term and its own information requirements. General causal frontiers under unknown and overlapping arrivals remain open. The schedule-information separation does not make every causal comparison impossible. Likewise, the one-step zero-remainder counterexample leaves room for comparisons with an explicit adaptation cost or a restricted performance family. Automatic precision, reward kernels with better tail behavior, a faithful adaptation of the original ALL-ε algorithms, and large-pool planning costs need further study. The supplement’s eventual exact-set consistency theorem belongs to a separate revisable multiresolution procedure under finite final arrivals and strict boundary separation. F-CCP’s coverage-event completion outside a boundary band is a different statement. Data and code availability The accompanying materials contain simulated data, frozen configurations, code, and the scripts used to generate the article’s tables and figures. The principal test has 27,648 recorded runs; a subsequent 1,152-run matched-cost ALL correction is retained separately, together with the superseded comparator. Replacing that comparator for the principal analysis leaves 24 configurations and 27,648 records. Earlier checkpoint comparisons contain 5,760 records and are reported separately in the supplement; the preceding CCP and frontier research suites retain their own protocols and archives. All reported failures remain in the analysis. The available implementation distinguishes the frozen dual-account production engine from the interactive interface and the development branches.
